opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I think a lot of founders underestimate. When you sell to a large enterprise, even a really big, bureaucratic one, there's usually a fairly clear path: you find a champion, you prove value in a pilot, and somebody with budget authority signs a contract. It can take six months, maybe a year, but the buyer and the user are often close to each other, and the money is relatively fungible.

With the military, those roles get pulled apart. The person who actually needs your technology, the operator in the field or the unit that's feeling the pain, usually isn't the person who controls the money. And the money itself is tied to a budget process that runs on a multi-year cycle. If you're not in the budget line two years out, it's very hard to just "buy" something at scale, no matter how much people love it. So you can have a hugely successful pilot, everyone's excited, and then you hit what people call the valley of death, where there's no program of record and no dedicated funding to carry you into production.

On top of that, you've got the acquisition regulations, security accreditation, getting your software onto classified networks, compliance requirements, and the fact that the customer's tolerance for risk is very different. When a commercial system fails, you lose revenue. When a military system fails, people can get hurt. So there's a natural conservatism built in.

The way I think about it is that you're not making one sale. You're navigating three or four parallel processes at once: the operational user, the requirements community, the acquisition and contracting folks, and ultimately Congress and the budget. Companies that succeed treat it as a long-term relationship and invest in understanding how the institution works, rather than expecting the enterprise playbook to carry over. That said, it's gotten better. Things like other transaction authorities, the Defense Innovation Unit, and more appetite for commercial technology have opened doors that weren't there ten years ago. It's still hard, but it's no longer impossible for a startup.

r001.rationale: The response presents large-enterprise sales as having a relatively clear path through a champion to a budget authority; it does not identify lack of unilateral authority as a central obstacle.

r002.rationale: It describes military sales as requiring several parallel stakeholder processes, while contrasting that with a clearer large-enterprise path. It does not characterize both as similarly requiring coalition building.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the two look similar on the surface and are completely different underneath.

With a large enterprise, you're usually selling to someone who can make a decision. There's a budget owner, there's a champion, and if you can show them the technology moves a number they care about, you can close in a quarter or two. The buyer and the user are often in the same building, sometimes the same person.

The military splits all of that apart. The person who wants the capability, say a unit commander or an operator who's seen your demo and is excited, almost never controls the money. The money sits in a program office, and that program office is working off budgets that were planned two or three years earlier. So even when everyone agrees you've solved a real problem, there may not be a line item for you. You end up living in pilots, small research contracts, these little bridges that keep you alive but don't scale.

The second difference is risk tolerance. A business will tolerate a product that's ninety percent there because the downside is a missed KPI. In the military, the downside can be someone's life, so the bar for trust is much higher, and rightly so. That means compliance, security accreditation, getting on the right networks. Those aren't afterthoughts. They can take longer than building the product.

And the third thing, which people underestimate, is that you're not just selling software, you're selling a change in how people work. A lot of these organizations have done things one way for decades. The technology is often the easy part. Getting it adopted, getting it into training, getting it into doctrine, that's the real sale.

So my framing is: with enterprise, you sell to a buyer. With the military, you sell to a system. You have to understand the system well enough to find where you fit, be patient enough to survive the timelines, and build something good enough that when the budget window finally opens, you're the obvious choice.

r001.rationale: It says enterprise sales usually involve someone who can make a decision and highlights divided authority in the military; it does not identify the absence of unilateral decision-making authority as an obstacle in large-business sales.

r002.rationale: It contrasts selling to an enterprise buyer with selling to a military system, but does not characterize both as requiring coalition building across stakeholders.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenges are more similar than people assume. In either case, you’re selling into a large organization where the person who uses your product may not be the person who controls the budget or approves the purchase. You can have someone who loves what you’ve built and still have a long way to go before you have a contract.

With the military, you also have to understand the acquisition process and the conditions in which the product will actually be used. A good demonstration is one thing; something people can rely on in the field is another. So the conversation has to start with their problem. What are they trying to accomplish, and how does your product help? That’s true in a large business, too. The technology gets you attention, but solving a problem is what makes the sale.

r001.rationale: The response says the product’s user may not control the budget or approve the purchase, identifying the lack of unilateral decision-making authority as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response compares the sales settings and notes that users, budget holders, and approvers may differ, but it does not communicate that selling requires building a coalition across those stakeholders.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest similarity is that neither one is a single customer. In a large business, the person using your product may be different from the person approving the purchase. The military has that same challenge: you have to understand who needs the capability, who controls the budget, and who can actually buy it.

You can have someone who loves what you’ve built and still have no clear path to a sale. So the job is more than demonstrating good technology. It’s understanding how that organization makes decisions and helping your customer navigate that process. And with the military, you also have to show that the product will work under the conditions where they actually need it.

r001.rationale: It says neither buyer is a single customer and distinguishes product users from purchase approvers, making divided decision authority a central obstacle.

r002.rationale: It identifies multiple military stakeholders and the need to navigate their process, but does not clearly say sellers must build a coalition across them.
